title: Hands-on Exercise 7b
section: Defining a function to read files from a folder
text:
Defining a function to read files from a folder
A function is created to read all files from a selected folder into a data frame. Each file is read line by line, and the file name is kept as the document ID. This makes it easier to combine multiple text files into a tidy data frame for analysis.


Show the code
read_folder <- function(infolder) {
  tibble(file = dir(infolder, full.names = TRUE)) %>%
    mutate(text = map(file, read_lines)) %>%
    transmute(id = basename(file), text) %>%
    unnest(text)
}

title: Hands-on Exercise 7b
section: Reading all messages from the 20news folder
text:
Reading all messages from the 20news folder
The code chunk below reads all the messages from the folders inside the 20news directory. Each folder represents a newsgroup, and the text files inside each folder are combined into one data frame. The final data frame includes the newsgroup name, document ID, and text content.


Show the code
raw_text <- tibble(folder = dir(news20, full.names = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(folder_out = map(folder, read_folder)) %>%
  unnest(cols = c(folder_out)) %>%
  transmute(newsgroup = basename(folder), 
            id, text)

dir.create("data/rds", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

write_rds(raw_text, "data/rds/news20.rds")


Important to note:

read_lines() from readr is used to read text files line by line.
map() from purrr is used to apply the read_folder() function to each folder.
unnest() is used to flatten the list-column into regular rows.
mutate() is used to create or modify variables while keeping existing variables.
transmute() is used to create new variables while dropping variables that are no longer needed.
write_rds() is used to save the combined data frame as an RDS file for future use.

title: Hands-on Exercise 7b
text:
Frequency of messages by newsgroup
The chart below shows the number of messages in each newsgroup. This helps us understand the distribution of documents across the different newsgroups before moving into text analysis.


Show the code
raw_text %>%
  group_by(newsgroup) %>%
  summarise(messages = n_distinct(id), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = messages, 
             y = reorder(newsgroup, messages))) +
  geom_col(fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(x = "Number of messages",
       y = "Newsgroup",
       title = "Frequency of Messages by Newsgroup") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Hands-on Exercise 7b
section: Removing headers and automated email signatures
text:
Removing headers and automated email signatures
Raw text messages often contain extra information that may not be useful for analysis, such as email headers, sender details, reply information, and automated signatures. These parts are removed so that the analysis focuses more on the actual message content.


Show the code
cleaned_text <- raw_text %>%
  group_by(newsgroup, id) %>%
  filter(cumsum(text == "") > 0,
         cumsum(str_detect(text, "^--")) == 0) %>%
  ungroup()


Important to note:

cumsum() is used to calculate cumulative sums and identify where the actual message content starts.
str_detect() from stringr is used to detect specific text patterns.

title: Hands-on Exercise 7b
section: Removing quoted text from other users
text:
Removing quoted text from other users
Some messages contain quoted replies from other users. These quoted lines can add noise to the analysis, so they are removed using regular expressions.


Show the code
cleaned_text <- cleaned_text %>%
  filter(str_detect(text, "^[^>]+[A-Za-z\\d]") | text == "",
         !str_detect(text, "writes(:|\\.\\.\\.)$"),
         !str_detect(text, "^In article <"))


Important to note:

filter() from dplyr is used to keep only the rows that meet the required conditions.
str_detect() is used to identify and remove lines that look like quoted text.

title: Hands-on Exercise 7b
text:
Tokenising and removing stop words
The cleaned text is split into individual words using unnest_tokens(). Stop words, such as common words like “the”, “and”, and “is”, are removed because they usually do not provide much meaning in text analysis.


Show the code
usenet_words <- cleaned_text %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  filter(str_detect(word, "[a-z']$"),
         !word %in% stop_words$word)

Counting common words
After cleaning and tokenising the text, we can count the most common words in the dataset.

title: Hands-on Exercise 7b
text:
Counting words by newsgroup
Instead of counting words across the entire dataset, words can also be counted within each newsgroup. This allows us to compare which words are more common in different topics.


Show the code
words_by_newsgroup <- usenet_words %>%
  count(newsgroup, word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  ungroup()

title: Hands-on Exercise 7b
text:
Static word cloud
A word cloud is used to visualise the most frequent words. Larger words represent words that appear more often in the dataset.


Show the code
wordcloud(words_by_newsgroup$word,
          words_by_newsgroup$n,
          max.words = 300)

title: Hands-on Exercise 7b
text:
Interactive table
An interactive DT table can be used to support the word cloud by allowing users to search, filter, and view the word frequency values more clearly.


Show the code
DT::datatable(words_by_newsgroup,
              filter = "top")

title: Hands-on Exercise 7b
text:
Word cloud by newsgroup
The ggwordcloud package is used to create word clouds by newsgroup. This makes it easier to compare common words across different newsgroup categories.


Show the code
set.seed(1234)

words_by_newsgroup %>%
  group_by(newsgroup) %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 30, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  ggplot(aes(label = word,
             size = n)) +
  geom_text_wordcloud() +
  theme_minimal() +
  facet_wrap(~newsgroup)

title: Hands-on Exercise 7b
text:
Computing TF-IDF within newsgroups
The bind_tf_idf() function from tidytext is used to calculate term frequency, inverse document frequency, and TF-IDF values.


Show the code
tf_idf <- words_by_newsgroup %>%
  bind_tf_idf(word, newsgroup, n) %>%
  arrange(desc(tf_idf))

title: Hands-on Exercise 7b
section: Visualising TF-IDF as an interactive table
text:
Visualising TF-IDF as an interactive table
An interactive table is created to display the TF-IDF results. This allows the values to be searched and filtered easily.


Show the code
DT::datatable(tf_idf, filter = "top") %>% 
  formatRound(columns = c("tf", "idf", "tf_idf"), 
              digits = 3) %>%
  formatStyle(0, 
              target = "row", 
              lineHeight = "25%")






Important to note:

filter = "top" adds filter boxes at the top of the table.
formatRound() is used to round the numeric values.
formatStyle() is used to adjust the appearance of the table.

title: Hands-on Exercise 7b
text:
Visualising TF-IDF within science newsgroups
A faceted bar chart is used to show the top TF-IDF words within science-related newsgroups. This helps to identify words that are more unique or important to each science topic.


Show the code
tf_idf %>%
  filter(str_detect(newsgroup, "^sci\\.")) %>%
  group_by(newsgroup) %>%
  slice_max(tf_idf, n = 12) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(word = reorder(word, tf_idf)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(tf_idf, word, fill = newsgroup)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ newsgroup, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "TF-IDF",
       y = NULL)

title: Hands-on Exercise 9a
text: I learned how to create choropleth maps in R using the tmap package, which is purpose-built for thematic mapping and offers far more cartographic control than general-purpose plotting packages. The quickest way to get a map on screen is qtm(), but building maps layer by layer with tm_shape(), tm_polygons(), tm_fill() and tm_borders() gives much finer control over classification, colour and layout. I also learned that the choice of data classification method (e.g. quantile vs equal) can change the visual story a map tells even when the underlying data is identical, which is an important reminder that “maps lie”. Finally, I practiced preparing small multiple choropleth maps in three different ways and learned how to subset spatial objects to map only a selected criterion.

title: Hands-on Exercise 9a
text:
The Data
Two data sets will be used to create the choropleth map:

Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary (Web) (i.e. MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL) in ESRI shapefile format, downloaded from data.gov.sg. This is a geospatial data set consisting of the geographical boundary of Singapore at the planning subzone level, based on URA Master Plan 2014.
Singapore Residents by Planning Area / Subzone, Age Group, Sex and Type of Dwelling, June 2011-2020 in csv format (i.e. respopagesextod2011to2020.csv), downloaded from the Department of Statistics, Singapore. This is an aspatial data file - although it does not contain coordinate values, its PA and SZ fields can be used as unique identifiers to geocode against the MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL shapefile.

title: Hands-on Exercise 9a
text:
Importing Attribute Data into R
Next, we import respopagesextod2011to2020.csv into RStudio and save the file into an R data frame called popdata, using read_csv() of readr package.


Show the code
popdata <- read_csv("data/respopagesextod2011to2020.csv")

title: Hands-on Exercise 9a
text:
Data Preparation
Before a thematic map can be prepared, we need a data table with year 2020 values, including the variables PA, SZ, YOUNG, ECONOMY ACTIVE, AGED, TOTAL and DEPENDENCY:

YOUNG: age group 0 to 4 until age group 20 to 24,
ECONOMY ACTIVE: age group 25-29 until age group 60-64,
AGED: age group 65 and above,
TOTAL: all age groups, and
DEPENDENCY: the ratio between young and aged against the economically active group.


Data wrangling
The following data wrangling and transformation functions are used: pivot_wider() of tidyr, and mutate(), filter(), group_by() and select() of dplyr.


Show the code
popdata2020 <- popdata %>%
  filter(Time == 2020) %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG) %>%
  summarise(`POP` = sum(`Pop`)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = AG,
              values_from = POP) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[3:6])
         + rowSums(.[12])) %>%
  mutate(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(.[7:11]) +
           rowSums(.[13:15])) %>%
  mutate(`AGED` = rowSums(.[16:21])) %>%
  mutate(`TOTAL` = rowSums(.[3:21])) %>%
  mutate(`DEPENDENCY` = (`YOUNG` + `AGED`)
         / `ECONOMY ACTIVE`) %>%
  select(`PA`, `SZ`, `YOUNG`,
         `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, `AGED`,
         `TOTAL`, `DEPENDENCY`)




Joining the attribute data and geospatial data
Before performing the georelational join, the values in the PA and SZ fields need to be converted to uppercase, since the SUBZONE_N and PLN_AREA_N fields in mpsz are already in uppercase.


Show the code
popdata2020 <- popdata2020 %>%
  mutate(across(c(PA, SZ), toupper)) %>%
  filter(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` > 0)


Next, left_join() of dplyr is used to join the geographical data and the attribute table using the planning subzone name (i.e. SUBZONE_N and SZ) as the common identifier.


Show the code
mpsz_pop2020 <- left_join(mpsz, popdata2020,
                           by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ"))


Using mpsz as the left data table in left_join() ensures that the output remains a simple features data frame.


Show the code
write_rds(mpsz_pop2020, "data/mpszpop2020.rds")

title: Hands-on Exercise 9a
section: Plotting a choropleth map quickly by using qtm()
text:
Plotting a choropleth map quickly by using qtm()
qtm() is the easiest and quickest way to draw a choropleth map using tmap. It is concise and provides a good default visualisation in many cases.


Show the code
tmap_mode("plot")
qtm(mpsz_pop2020,
    fill = "DEPENDENCY")










tmap_mode() with the “plot” option produces a static map; for interactive mode, “view” should be used instead.
The fill argument maps the attribute of interest (i.e. DEPENDENCY).

title: Hands-on Exercise 9a
section: Creating a choropleth map by using tmap’s elements
text:
Creating a choropleth map by using tmap’s elements
While qtm() is quick, it makes it harder to control the aesthetics of individual layers. To draw a higher quality cartographic choropleth map, tmap’s drawing elements are used instead.


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: Planning Sub-zone boundary from Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA)\n and Population data from Department of Statistics DOS",
             position = c("left", "bottom"))










Drawing a base map
The basic building block of tmap is tm_shape() followed by one or more layer elements such as tm_fill() and tm_polygons().


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons()











Drawing a choropleth map using tm_polygons()
To draw a choropleth map showing the geographical distribution of a selected variable by planning subzone, the target variable (i.e. DEPENDENCY) is simply assigned to tm_polygons().


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY")










The default interval binning method used is “pretty”.
The default colour scheme is YlOrRd of ColorBrewer.
Missing values are shaded grey by default.



Drawing a choropleth map using tm_fill() and tm_borders()
tm_polygons() is actually a wrapper of tm_fill() and tm_borders(). tm_fill() shades the polygons using the default colour scheme, and tm_borders() adds the shapefile’s borders onto the choropleth map.


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY")









To add the boundary of the planning subzones, tm_borders() is used:


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders(lwd = 0.01,
             fill_alpha = 0.1)









tm_borders() supports several arguments: col for border colour, lwd for line width (default 1), and lty for line type (default “solid”).

title: Hands-on Exercise 9a
text:
Data classification methods of tmap
tmap provides ten data classification methods: fixed, sd, equal, pretty (default), quantile, kmeans, hclust, bclust, fisher and jenks. The classification method is defined using the style argument of tm_fill() or tm_polygons().

Plotting choropleth maps with built-in classification methods
The code chunk below uses the jenks classification with 5 classes.


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        style = "jenks",
        n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)









The code chunk below uses the equal classification method instead.


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        style = "equal",
        n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)









The quantile classification distributes the data more evenly across classes than the equal classification method, which is a useful reminder that maps can present the same underlying data very differently depending on the classification chosen.


Plotting choropleth map with custom breaks
For built-in styles, category breaks are computed internally. To override these defaults, breakpoints can be set explicitly using the breaks argument of tm_fill(). In tmap, breaks include a minimum and maximum, so n+1 elements must be specified to produce n categories.


Show the code
summary(mpsz_pop2020$DEPENDENCY)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
 0.1111  0.7147  0.7867  0.8585  0.8763 19.0000      92 


Based on the summary statistics, break points are set at 0.60, 0.70, 0.80 and 0.90, together with a minimum of 0 and a maximum of 1.00.


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
          breaks = c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

title: Hands-on Exercise 9a
text:
Colour Scheme
tmap supports colour ramps either defined by the user or a set of predefined colour ramps from the RColorBrewer package.

Using ColourBrewer palette
To change the colour, the preferred colour is assigned to the values argument of tm_scale_intervals().


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        style = "quantile",
        n = 5,
        values = "brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)









To reverse the colour shading, a “-” prefix is added.


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        style = "quantile",
        n = 5,
        values = "-brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

title: Hands-on Exercise 9a
text:
Map Layouts
Map layout refers to the combination of all map elements into a cohesive map, including the objects mapped, title, scale bar, compass, margins and aspect ratio.

Map Legend
tm_legend() provides options to change the placement, format and appearance of the legend.


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("DEPENDENCY",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        style = "jenks",
        n = 5,
        values = "brewer.greens"),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
        title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone \n(Jenks classification)")











Map style
tmap_style() allows a wide variety of layout settings to be changed. The code chunk below uses the classic style.


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          style = "quantile",
          palette = "-Greens") +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("classic")











Cartographic Furniture
tm_compass(), tm_scale_bar() and tm_grid() are used to add a compass, scale bar and grid lines onto the choropleth map.


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: Planning Sub-zone boundary from Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA)\n and Population data from Department of Statistics DOS",
             position = c("left", "bottom"))









To reset the default style:


Show the code
tmap_style("white")

title: Hands-on Exercise 9a
text:
Drawing Small Multiple Choropleth Maps
Small multiple maps, also known as facet maps, are composed of many maps arranged side-by-side or stacked vertically, enabling visualisation of how spatial relationships change with respect to another variable, such as time. In tmap, small multiple maps can be plotted in three ways: by assigning multiple values to at least one aesthetic argument, by defining a group-by variable in tm_facets(), or by creating multiple stand-alone maps with tmap_arrange().

By assigning multiple values to at least one aesthetic argument


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill(c("YOUNG", "AGED"),
          style = "equal",
          palette = "Blues") +
  tm_layout(legend.position = c("right", "bottom")) +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("white")











Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons(c("DEPENDENCY", "AGED"),
          style = c("equal", "quantile"),
          palette = list("Blues", "Greens")) +
  tm_layout(legend.position = c("right", "bottom"))











By defining a group-by variable in tm_facets()


Show the code
tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          style = "quantile",
          palette = "Blues",
          thres.poly = 0) +
  tm_facets(by = "REGION_N",
            free.coords = TRUE) +
  tm_layout(legend.show = FALSE,
            title.position = c("center", "center"),
            title.size = 20) +
  tm_borders(alpha = 0.5)











By creating multiple stand-alone maps with tmap_arrange()


Show the code
youngmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("YOUNG",
              style = "quantile",
              palette = "Blues")

agedmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2020) +
  tm_polygons("AGED",
              style = "quantile",
              palette = "Blues")

tmap_arrange(youngmap, agedmap, asp = 1, ncol = 2)

title: Hands-on Exercise 9a
section: Mapping Spatial Objects Meeting a Selection Criterion
text:
Mapping Spatial Objects Meeting a Selection Criterion
Instead of creating small multiple choropleth maps, a selection function can be used to map only spatial objects meeting a selection criterion - in this case, subzones within the Central Region.


Show the code

title: Hands-on Exercise 9c
text: I learned that mapping counts directly can be misleading because the underlying phenomenon, in this case water points, is not evenly distributed in space; mapping rates (e.g. percentage functional) instead of raw counts gives a fairer picture. I also learned how extreme value maps such as percentile maps and box maps are designed to highlight outliers at the low and high ends of a distribution, which is a useful complement to standard choropleth classification methods like quantile or equal. Writing small reusable R functions such as get.var(), percentmap(), boxbreaks() and boxmap() also showed me how functions reduce repetition and the risk of copy-paste mistakes when the same logic needs to be applied to multiple variables.

title: Hands-on Exercise 9c
text:
Percentile Map
The percentile map is a special type of quantile map with six specific categories: 0-1%, 1-10%, 10-50%, 50-90%, 90-99%, and 99-100%. The corresponding breakpoints can be derived using the base R quantile() function, passing an explicit vector of cumulative probabilities as c(0, .01, .1, .5, .9, .99, 1). Note that the begin and end points need to be included.

Data Preparation
Step 1: Exclude records with NA.


Show the code
NGA_wp <- NGA_wp %>%
  drop_na()


Step 2: Create a customised classification and extract the values.


Show the code
percent <- c(0, .01, .1, .5, .9, .99, 1)
var <- NGA_wp["pct_functional"] %>%
  st_set_geometry(NULL)
quantile(var[, 1], percent)


       0%        1%       10%       50%       90%       99%      100% 
0.0000000 0.0000000 0.2169811 0.4791667 0.8611111 1.0000000 1.0000000 


Note: When variables are extracted from an sf data frame, the geometry is extracted as well. For mapping and spatial manipulation this is expected behaviour, but many base R functions cannot deal with the geometry - specifically, quantile() will return an error. As a result, st_set_geometry(NULL) is used to drop the geometry field.


Why writing functions?
Writing a function has three big advantages over copy-and-paste:

It can be given an evocative name that makes the code easier to understand.
As requirements change, code only needs to be updated in one place instead of many.
It eliminates the chance of making incidental mistakes when copying and pasting (e.g. updating a variable name in one place but not another).



Creating the get.var function
An R function is written below to extract a variable (e.g. wp_nonfunctional) as a vector out of an sf data frame.

Arguments: vname (variable name as character, in quotes), df (name of sf data frame).
Returns: v, a vector of values without a column name.



Show the code
get.var <- function(vname, df) {
  v <- df[vname] %>%
    st_set_geometry(NULL)
  v <- unname(v[, 1])
  return(v)
}




A percentile mapping function
Next, a percentile mapping function is written using the code chunk below.


Show the code
percentmap <- function(vnam, df, legtitle = NA, mtitle = "Percentile Map") {
  percent <- c(0, .01, .1, .5, .9, .99, 1)
  var <- get.var(vnam, df)
  bperc <- quantile(var, percent)
  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons() +
  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons(vnam,
            title = legtitle,
            breaks = bperc,
            palette = "Blues",
            labels = c("< 1%", "1% - 10%", "10% - 50%",
                       "50% - 90%", "90% - 99%", "> 99%")) +
    tm_borders() +
    tm_layout(main.title = mtitle,
              title.position = c("right", "bottom"))
}




Test drive the percentile mapping function


Show the code
percentmap("total_wp", NGA_wp)









Note that this is just a bare-bones implementation - additional arguments such as the title and legend positioning could be passed to customise other features of the map.

title: Hands-on Exercise 9c
text:
Box map
In essence, a box map is an augmented quartile map with an additional lower and upper category. When there are lower outliers, the starting point for the breaks is the minimum value, and the second break is the lower fence. When there are no lower outliers, the starting point for the breaks is the lower fence, and the second break is the minimum value (there will be no observations falling between the lower fence and the minimum value).


Show the code
ggplot(data = NGA_wp,
       aes(x = "",
           y = wp_nonfunctional)) +
  geom_boxplot()









A box map displays summary statistics on a choropleth map by using the basic principles of a boxplot. To create one, a custom breaks specification is needed - this is more complex than it sounds, because the break points vary depending on whether lower or upper outliers are present.

Creating the boxbreaks function
The code chunk below is an R function that creates break points for a box map.

Arguments: v (vector of observations), mult (multiplier for IQR, default 1.5).
Returns: bb, a vector with 7 break points computed from the quartiles and fences.



Show the code
boxbreaks <- function(v, mult = 1.5) {
  qv <- unname(quantile(v))
  iqr <- qv[4] - qv[2]
  upfence <- qv[4] + mult * iqr
  lofence <- qv[2] - mult * iqr
  # initialize break points vector
  bb <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = 7)
  # logic for lower and upper fences
  if (lofence < qv[1]) {  # no lower outliers
    bb[1] <- lofence
    bb[2] <- floor(qv[1])
  } else {
    bb[2] <- lofence
    bb[1] <- qv[1]
  }
  if (upfence > qv[5]) { # no upper outliers
    bb[7] <- upfence
    bb[6] <- ceiling(qv[5])
  } else {
    bb[6] <- upfence
    bb[7] <- qv[5]
  }
  bb[3:5] <- qv[2:4]
  return(bb)
}




Creating the get.var function
The code chunk below is an R function to extract a variable as a vector out of an sf data frame.

Arguments: vname (variable name as character, in quotes), df (name of sf data frame).
Returns: v, a vector of values without a column name.



Show the code
get.var <- function(vname, df) {
  v <- df[vname] %>% st_set_geometry(NULL)
  v <- unname(v[, 1])
  return(v)
}




Test drive the newly created function


Show the code
var <- get.var("wp_nonfunctional", NGA_wp)
boxbreaks(var)


[1] -56.5   0.0  14.0  34.0  61.0 131.5 278.0




Boxmap function
The code chunk below is an R function to create a box map.

Arguments: vnam (variable name as character, in quotes), df (simple features polygon layer), legtitle (legend title), mtitle (map title), mult (multiplier for IQR).
Returns: a tmap element that plots a map.



Show the code
boxmap <- function(vnam, df,
                    legtitle = NA,
                    mtitle = "Box Map",
                    mult = 1.5) {
  var <- get.var(vnam, df)
  bb <- boxbreaks(var)
  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons() +
  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_fill(vnam, title = legtitle,
            breaks = bb,
            palette = "Blues",
            labels = c("lower outlier",
                       "< 25%",
                       "25% - 50%",
                       "50% - 75%",
                       "> 75%",
                       "upper outlier")) +
    tm_borders() +
    tm_layout(main.title = mtitle,
              title.position = c("left", "top"))
}




Show the code
tmap_mode("plot")
boxmap("wp_nonfunctional", NGA_wp)

title: Analytical Computation
text:
Data Preparation and Exploration established the shape of the data and turned up two loose threads worth pulling on. First, the timeline visibly breaks in two — a steady, daily-cadence “baseline” period (rounds 1–13) followed by an hourly “crisis day” (rounds 14–23) — but that break was only ever shown as a volume spike, not measured. Second, the private-sentiment chart suggested that at least one agent’s internal alarm rose before its content showed up on an unmonitored channel, which is exactly the kind of lead-indicator a leak investigation wants, but it was never tested agent by agent.
This page does both. It builds a per-round deviation index that measures, numerically, how far each round’s channel mix has drifted from the pre-crisis baseline, and it compares each agent’s first negative-sentiment round against their first unmonitored merger mention to see whether private alarm actually predicts the leak, or just coincides with it.


Show the code

               tidygraph, ggraph, igraph, tidytext, textdata)

`%||%` <- function(x, y) if (is.null(x) || length(x) == 0) y else x

title: Analytical Computation
text:
2 Rebuilding the working tables
The flattening logic is unchanged from the preparation page — it is repeated here only so this page renders on its own, not because the approach has changed. See Data Preparation and Exploration for the full explanation of each step.


Show the code
mc1_raw <- fromJSON("data/MC1_final_00.json", simplifyDataFrame = FALSE)
rounds_raw <- mc1_raw$rounds

agent_levels <- c("legal_agent","quality_agent","pr_agent","social_media_agent",
                   "pr_intern_agent","intern_agent","judge_agent")
channel_levels <- c("comms_huddle","one_on_one_chat","side_huddle",
                     "official_post","personal_post","anonymous_post")
agent_display <- c(
  legal_agent = "Legal", quality_agent = "Platform Trust", pr_agent = "PR",
  social_media_agent = "Social Media", pr_intern_agent = "PR Intern",
  intern_agent = "Intern", judge_agent = "Judge")

flatten_message <- function(m, round_idx, round_hour) {
  recipients <- m$recipients %||% character(0)
  tibble(
    round_idx      = round_idx,
    round_hour     = round_hour,
    message_id     = m$message_id,
    agent_id       = m$agent_id,
    channel        = m$channel,
    message_type   = m$message_type,
    recipients_csv = if (length(recipients) == 0) NA_character_
                      else paste(recipients, collapse = ";"),
    recipients_is_all = "ALL" %in% recipients,
    content        = m$content %||% "",
    reacting       = m$internal_state$reacting %||% NA_character_,
    rationalizing  = m$internal_state$rationalizing %||% NA_character_,
    deliberating   = m$internal_state$deliberating %||% NA_character_
  )
}

messages_tbl <- map_dfr(seq_along(rounds_raw), function(i) {
  rd <- rounds_raw[[i]]
  map_dfr(rd$communications %||% list(), flatten_message,
           round_idx = i, round_hour = rd$hour)
}) %>%
  mutate(
    agent_id      = factor(agent_id, levels = agent_levels),
    channel       = factor(channel, levels = channel_levels),
    round_hour_dt = ymd_hms(round_hour)
  )

recipient_to_agent <- c(
  legal = "legal_agent", platform_trust = "quality_agent", pr = "pr_agent",
  social_manager = "social_media_agent", pr_intern = "pr_intern_agent",
  intern = "intern_agent", judge = "judge_agent")

topic_patterns <- tribble(
  ~topic,   ~pattern,
  "Merger", "\\b(merger|civicloom|harborcrest|acquisition|deal)\\b"
)
tag_topics <- function(text) {
  text <- str_to_lower(text)
  topic_patterns$topic[map_lgl(topic_patterns$pattern, ~ str_detect(text, .x))]
}

messages_tbl <- messages_tbl %>%
  mutate(
    topics         = map(content, tag_topics),
    is_merger      = map_lgl(topics, ~ "Merger" %in% .x),
    is_unmonitored = channel %in% c("side_huddle","official_post","personal_post","anonymous_post")
  )

agent_nodes <- tibble(name = agent_levels) %>%
  mutate(label = recode(name, !!!agent_display))

nrow(messages_tbl)


[1] 912

title: Analytical Computation
text:
3 Defining the two periods
The split is the one the volume chart on the preparation page already pointed to: rounds 1–13 run days apart with a daily headline, rounds 14–23 are hourly on a single crisis day, 5 June 2046. That structural seam, not a fixed calendar date, is what “baseline” and “crisis day” mean for the rest of this page.


Show the code
messages_tbl <- messages_tbl %>%
  mutate(period = if_else(round_idx <= 13, "Baseline", "Crisis day"))

messages_tbl %>%
  count(period) %>%
  kable()

title: Analytical Computation
text:
4 Channel-mix deviation
If the crisis genuinely changed how agents communicate, the share of traffic on each channel — not just the raw count — should shift between the two periods. Comparing proportions rather than counts also controls for the simple fact that the crisis day has more messages overall.


Show the code
library(scales)

channel_mix <- messages_tbl %>%
  count(period, channel) %>%
  group_by(period) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup()

ggplot(channel_mix, aes(x = channel, y = share, fill = period)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.7) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(Baseline = "#4A5568", `Crisis day` = "#C05621"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Share of messages",
    title = "Channel mix: baseline vs. crisis day"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "top"
  )











Show the code
monitored_share <- messages_tbl %>%
  mutate(monitored = channel %in% c("comms_huddle","one_on_one_chat")) %>%
  count(period, monitored) %>%
  group_by(period) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(monitored) %>%
  select(period, monitored_share = share)

monitored_share %>% kable()





period
monitored_share




Baseline
0.8920863


Crisis day
0.7111111





The unmonitored share of traffic grows on the crisis day, but only modestly — most of the extra volume is still happening on monitored ground. That is consistent with the preparation page’s finding that the merger discussion itself mostly stayed on monitored channels; the unmonitored share is small enough that a handful of genuine leak messages can sit inside it without moving the aggregate number much, which is exactly why a per-round, rather than per-period, view is needed next.

title: Analytical Computation
text:
5 A per-round deviation index
To find which rounds actually drift from normal, each round’s channel-mix vector is compared against the average baseline mix using a simple Euclidean distance across the six channel shares. A round identical to the baseline mix scores 0; a round where traffic moves to channels rarely used at baseline scores higher.


Show the code
channel_share_by_round <- messages_tbl %>%
  count(round_idx, channel) %>%
  complete(round_idx = 1:23, channel = channel_levels, fill = list(n = 0)) %>%
  group_by(round_idx) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup()

baseline_share <- channel_share_by_round %>%
  filter(round_idx <= 13) %>%
  group_by(channel) %>%
  summarise(baseline_share = mean(share), .groups = "drop")

deviation_idx <- channel_share_by_round %>%
  left_join(baseline_share, by = "channel") %>%
  mutate(sq_diff = (share - baseline_share)^2) %>%
  group_by(round_idx) %>%
  summarise(deviation = sqrt(sum(sq_diff)), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(deviation_idx, aes(x = round_idx, y = deviation)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#9B2C2C", width = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 13.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:23) +
  labs(x = "Round", y = "Deviation from baseline channel mix",
       title = "Which rounds drift furthest from normal communication patterns") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())











Show the code
deviation_idx %>%
  arrange(desc(deviation)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5) %>%
  left_join(messages_tbl %>% distinct(round_idx, round_hour_dt), by = "round_idx") %>%
  kable()

title: Analytical Computation
text:
6 Network structure: before vs. during
The same directed-network construction from the preparation page is run twice — once on baseline rounds only, once on crisis-day rounds only — to see whether the crisis reshapes who talks to whom, or only adds volume on top of the same structure.


Show the code
build_period_graph <- function(df) {
  edges <- df %>%
    filter(!recipients_is_all, !is.na(recipients_csv)) %>%
    separate_rows(recipients_csv, sep = ";") %>%
    filter(recipients_csv %in% names(recipient_to_agent)) %>%
    mutate(from = as.character(agent_id), to = recipient_to_agent[recipients_csv]) %>%
    filter(from != to) %>%
    count(from, to, name = "weight")

  tbl_graph(nodes = agent_nodes, edges = edges, directed = TRUE) %>%
    mutate(
      in_weight   = centrality_degree(weights = weight, mode = "in"),
      betweenness = centrality_betweenness(weights = 1 / weight, directed = TRUE)
    )
}

baseline_graph <- build_period_graph(messages_tbl %>% filter(period == "Baseline"))
crisis_graph   <- build_period_graph(messages_tbl %>% filter(period == "Crisis day"))

period_centrality <- bind_rows(
  baseline_graph %>% as_tibble() %>% mutate(period = "Baseline"),
  crisis_graph   %>% as_tibble() %>% mutate(period = "Crisis day")
) %>%
  select(period, label, in_weight, betweenness) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = c(in_weight, betweenness)) %>%
  mutate(betweenness_change = `betweenness_Crisis day` - betweenness_Baseline) %>%
  arrange(desc(betweenness_change))

period_centrality %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2))) %>%
  kable()

title: Analytical Computation
text:
7 Deepening the leak investigation
The preparation page scored each agent’s private monologue with AFINN and flagged that at least one agent’s sentiment turned negative early. Here that is made precise: for every agent, find the first round their mean private sentiment drops below zero, and separately the first round any of their messages is both merger-related and posted to an unmonitored channel. The gap between those two rounds is the test of whether private alarm is a leading indicator of the leak, or just noise that happens to overlap with it.


Show the code
internal_text <- messages_tbl %>%
  filter(!is.na(reacting) | !is.na(rationalizing) | !is.na(deliberating)) %>%
  mutate(internal_monologue = paste(reacting, rationalizing, deliberating)) %>%
  select(round_idx, agent_id, internal_monologue) %>%
  mutate(row_id = row_number())

afinn <- get_sentiments("afinn")

monologue_sentiment <- internal_text %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, internal_monologue) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") %>%
  inner_join(afinn, by = "word") %>%
  group_by(row_id) %>%
  summarise(score = sum(value), .groups = "drop") %>%
  right_join(internal_text, by = "row_id") %>%
  mutate(score = replace_na(score, 0))

round_sentiment <- monologue_sentiment %>%
  group_by(round_idx, agent_id) %>%
  summarise(mean_score = mean(score), .groups = "drop")




Show the code
alarm_round <- round_sentiment %>%
  filter(agent_id != "judge_agent", mean_score < 0) %>%
  group_by(agent_id) %>%
  summarise(alarm_round = min(round_idx), .groups = "drop")

leak_round <- messages_tbl %>%
  filter(is_merger, is_unmonitored) %>%
  group_by(agent_id) %>%
  summarise(leak_round = min(round_idx), .groups = "drop")

evidence_gap <- alarm_round %>%
  inner_join(leak_round, by = "agent_id") %>%
  mutate(
    agent = recode(as.character(agent_id), !!!agent_display),
    gap   = leak_round - alarm_round

ggplot(evidence_gap, aes(y = reorder(agent, -gap))) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = alarm_round, xend = leak_round, yend = agent),
               colour = "grey60", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(x = alarm_round, colour = "First negative-sentiment round"), size = 3) +
  geom_point(aes(x = leak_round, colour = "First unmonitored merger mention"), size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("First negative-sentiment round" = "#2C5282",
                                  "First unmonitored merger mention" = "#9B2C2C"),
                       name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Round", y = NULL,
       title = "Private alarm vs. the first unmonitored merger mention, by agent") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Only the agents who have both a negative-sentiment round and an unmonitored merger mention appear here, so this is a small, deliberately narrow comparison rather than a claim about all seven agents. Where the blue point sits to the left of the red point, that agent’s private alarm rose before their content reached an unmonitored channel — the order the leading-indicator hypothesis predicts. Where the two rounds are equal or reversed, sentiment and the leak move together rather than one predicting the other, which is a weaker basis for attribution. Cross-referencing this table against the round numbers already flagged on the preparation page (round 17 and round 22) is the most direct way to check whether the agent named there is also the agent whose alarm rose earliest.

title: Analytical Computation
text:
8 Summary
The crisis day is a measurable, not just visible, deviation from baseline: channel mix shifts modestly overall but sharply in a handful of specific rounds, and the communication network keeps the same hub — Legal — while routing more traffic through it. The alarm-versus-leak comparison gives a concrete, falsifiable test of the preparation page’s closing hypothesis, rather than leaving it as a visual impression from two separate charts. The Findings page pulls these results together with the specific message content into a single attribution.

title: Findings
text:
Two earlier pages built up to this one. Data Preparation and Exploration flattened the raw timeline, ranked the six communication channels by how visible they are to the Judge, and turned up two messages that discuss the embargoed merger on a fully public, unmonitored channel before the embargo’s 6:00 PM deadline. Analytical Computation made that finding rigorous: it measured exactly how far each round drifts from normal communication patterns, confirmed that the agent network’s structural hub does not change between the calm period and the crisis day, and tested whether any agent’s private alarm rises before their content reaches an unmonitored channel.
This page pulls those threads into one timeline and states a conclusion: who most likely broke the embargo, and when the leak actually happened relative to when it was supposed to.

flatten_message <- function(m, round_idx, round_hour) {
  recipients <- m$recipients %||% character(0)
  tibble(

    round_hour     = round_hour,
    agent_id       = m$agent_id,

  )

messages_tbl <- map_dfr(seq_along(rounds_raw), function(i) {

  )

channel_share_by_round <- messages_tbl %>%
  count(round_idx, channel) %>%
  complete(round_idx = 1:23, channel = channel_levels, fill = list(n = 0)) %>%
  group_by(round_idx) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup()

baseline_share <- channel_share_by_round %>%
  filter(round_idx <= 13) %>%
  group_by(channel) %>%
  summarise(baseline_share = mean(share), .groups = "drop")

deviation_idx <- channel_share_by_round %>%
  left_join(baseline_share, by = "channel") %>%
  mutate(sq_diff = (share - baseline_share)^2) %>%
  group_by(round_idx) %>%
  summarise(deviation = sqrt(sum(sq_diff)), .groups = "drop")

leak_candidates <- messages_tbl %>%
  filter(is_merger, is_unmonitored) %>%
  select(round_idx, round_hour_dt, agent_id, channel, content) %>%
  arrange(round_hour_dt)

pre_embargo_leaks <- leak_candidates %>%
  filter(round_idx < 23, channel %in% c("anonymous_post","personal_post"))

title: Findings
text:
4 Why this agent, structurally
The analytical page’s network comparison adds the structural piece: Legal is the most central agent in the communication network even before the crisis starts, and that position does not shift to anyone else once the crisis day begins — it only carries more traffic. An agent sitting at the structural center of the team’s internal coordination is, by construction, exposed to more of what is happening across every other agent’s workstream than a peripheral agent would be. That does not by itself prove who leaked; it explains how an agent in that seat would have had the full picture early enough to leak it.
The sentiment-versus-leak comparison is the corroborating signal, not the deciding one: where an agent’s private alarm rises before their content reaches an unmonitored channel, that ordering is consistent with someone privately recognizing the severity of the situation ahead of acting publicly on it, rather than reacting in the moment. Reading the round numbers from the Analytical Computation alarm-vs-leak table alongside the round 17 and round 22 dates above is the direct check on whether that same agent’s sentiment also turned earliest.

title: Findings
text:
5 Verdict
The strongest, most defensible claim the data supports is this: the embargo was broken at least twice before its scheduled lift, both times on the same fully public, unmonitored channel, both times traced to the same sending agent, and that agent occupies the most structurally central position in the team’s internal network throughout the entire timeline — meaning they were positioned to know the most, earliest, of anyone on the team.
What the data does not support is a motive. Nothing in the message content, the network structure, or the sentiment trend explains why that agent chose to disclose the deal early rather than simply being the best-informed person on the team. That is the natural next question for the dataset, and it would need to come from a closer reading of that agent’s own rationalizing and deliberating text in the rounds immediately before round 17, rather than from any of the aggregate measures used across these three pages.

title: Executive Summary
section: Motor Insurance Portfolio Profitability and Volatility
text:
Motor Insurance Portfolio Profitability and Volatility
Executive Summary

Serene Cheng
ISSS608 Visual Analytics and Applications
May 2026


This presentation summarises the key findings from my take-home exercise on a Spanish motor insurance portfolio. The focus is on understanding portfolio profitability and volatility using visual analytics and statistical validation. Instead of presenting every chart from the technical report, this executive summary highlights the main business patterns that matter for decision-making: portfolio composition, profitability movement, risk segments, claim frequency and claim severity.

title: Executive Summary
text:
Contents



Business context and objective

Data and analytical approach

Portfolio composition

Policyholder and vehicle profile

Profitability overview

Policy type and loss ratio



Profitability trend over time

Business type and underwriting profit

Bonus score pattern

Claim frequency

Claim severity

Recommendations and conclusion



I will first introduce the business context and data approach, then highlight the main visual findings. The middle slides focus on profitability because this is the key business outcome. The later slides cover claim frequency and claim severity, which help explain portfolio volatility. I end with recommendations that the insurer can consider for pricing, underwriting and further investigation.

title: Executive Summary
text:
1. Business Context and Objective
Insurers need to understand which portfolio segments drive poor profitability and claim volatility.
This study aims to:

Explore policy, driver, vehicle and geographic characteristics
Analyse profitability using loss ratio and underwriting profit
Analyse volatility using claim frequency and claim severity
Validate key visual patterns using statistical tests


The business problem is that poor profitability in an insurance portfolio may not be caused by one obvious factor. It can be influenced by policy coverage, customer profile, vehicle characteristics, claim behaviour and changes over time. Therefore, the objective is not just to describe the dataset, but to identify which segments appear linked to weaker profitability or higher volatility. Loss ratio is used as the main profitability indicator, while claim frequency and claim severity are used to understand claim behaviour.

title: Executive Summary
text:
2. Data and Analytical Approach
Dataset used:

Spanish motor insurance portfolio
354,140 raw records
1,802 rows removed due to missing values
Final analysis focused on selected policy, vehicle, claim and premium variables

Derived measures:

loss_ratio = total_incurred / total_premium
underwriting_profit = total_premium - total_incurred
claim_frequency = total_claims / total_exposure
claim_severity = total_incurred / total_claims


The raw dataset contains more than 354,000 policy-year records. After removing missing values, only around 0.51% of records were dropped, so the data loss is small. I derived several insurance measures to support the analysis. Loss ratio shows how much of premium is used to cover claims. Underwriting profit gives a simplified profitability view before expenses and other adjustments. Claim frequency measures how often claims occur after adjusting for exposure, while claim severity measures the average claim amount when claims occur.

title: Executive Summary
text:
3. Portfolio Composition: Policy Type

Key insight:

CC policies dominate the portfolio at 204,317 policies (58.0%)
COMP_E is second largest at 90,320 policies (25.6%)
TP and COMP_N form smaller shares


This chart shows that the portfolio is highly concentrated in CC policies, which make up 58% of the portfolio. This means the insurer’s exposure is mainly in broader coverage products rather than basic third-party-only policies. This is important because policy mix can affect both premium level and claim cost. Even if some policy types are smaller in count, they may still be important if they have weaker profitability or higher loss-making shares.

title: Executive Summary
text:
4. Policyholder and Vehicle Profile






















Key insight:

Drivers are mostly concentrated between 35 and 65 years old
Vehicle value is right-skewed, with median 24,687 and mean 26,937
High-value vehicles may contribute to higher claim severity even if they form a smaller group


The portfolio mainly consists of middle-aged drivers, with fewer very young or very old drivers. Vehicle value is right-skewed, meaning most vehicles are lower to mid-value, while a smaller number of high-value vehicles pull the mean upward. This matters because high-value vehicles may not dominate the portfolio by count, but they could still contribute to larger claim amounts if accidents occur. However, later correlation results suggest that continuous variables such as age and vehicle value are not strong standalone predictors.

title: Executive Summary
text:
5. Profitability Overview: Loss Ratio Groups

Key insight:

Most policies fall under No Loss
Smaller group is Profitable / Acceptable
Loss-making group is smaller but important


The loss ratio distribution is zero-heavy because many insurance policies do not record claims within the exposure period. This is expected in insurance portfolios. However, the smaller loss-making group is still important because these policies have incurred claims greater than premiums collected. From a management perspective, the key issue is not just how many policies are loss-making, but whether specific segments have a higher concentration of these policies.

title: Executive Summary
section: 6. Policy Type and Loss Ratio Group
text:
6. Policy Type and Loss Ratio Group

Key insight:

COMP_N has the highest loss-making share at 20.8%
TP and TPG perform better, with 94.7% and 91.2% no-loss policies
Chi-square test confirms significant association:
χ² = 7921.4, p < 0.001


This is one of the strongest business findings. Policy type is significantly associated with loss ratio group. COMP_N has the highest loss-making share, suggesting that this policy type may need closer pricing or underwriting review. In contrast, TP and TPG show very high no-loss shares, which suggests stronger profitability performance. The Chi-square test supports that the difference across policy types is statistically significant and not just a visual pattern.

title: Executive Summary
text:
7. Profitability Trend Over Time

Key insight:

Average loss ratio increased from 0.67 in 2022
To 0.73 in 2023
To 0.87 in 2024
Still below break-even point of 1.00, but moving closer


The portfolio is still profitable on average because the loss ratio remains below 1.00. However, the upward trend is a warning sign. Average loss ratio increased from 0.67 in 2022 to 0.87 in 2024, meaning a larger share of premium is being used to cover incurred claims. Pairwise Wilcoxon tests show that loss ratio differs significantly across all year pairs, with adjusted p-values below 0.001. This suggests that profitability has weakened meaningfully over time.

title: Executive Summary
text:
8. Business Type and Underwriting Profit

Key insight:

Portfolio policies show higher underwriting profit than New Business policies
Wilcoxon test confirms significant difference: p < 0.001
Existing policies may be more profitable than newly acquired policies


This slide compares underwriting profit between new business and existing portfolio policies. The finding suggests that portfolio policies perform better than new business policies. This may happen because existing policies have more stable risk profiles, better pricing history or improved renewal selection. The Wilcoxon test confirms that the difference is statistically significant. For the insurer, this means acquisition growth should be monitored carefully to ensure that new business is not weakening overall profitability.

title: Executive Summary
text:
9. Bonus Score and Underwriting Profit

Key insight:

Good bonus score dominates the portfolio at 96.5%
Underwriting profit differs significantly across bonus score groups
Kruskal-Wallis result: H(2) = 977.21, p < 0.001
Bad group shows highest median profit, but group size is small


This finding is interesting because it is counterintuitive. We might expect better bonus scores to always show higher profitability, but the Bad group shows the highest median underwriting profit. However, this should not be over-interpreted because the Bad group is very small compared with the Good group. The result may be affected by pricing, coverage mix or small-group effects. The statistical test shows that the groups differ significantly, but further investigation is needed before making business decisions.

title: Executive Summary
text:
10. Claim Frequency

Key insight:

301,814 policies (85.7%) have no claims
17,911 policies (5.1%) have low claim frequency
32,565 policies (9.2%) have high claim frequency


Claim frequency is also zero-heavy, which is normal for motor insurance because most policyholders do not make claims in a given period. The majority of policies fall under the no-claim group. However, the high claim frequency group still matters because repeated claims can create volatility and may signal riskier behaviour or exposure. This slide helps separate claim occurrence from claim size, which is important because profitability pressure can come from either frequent claims or severe claims.

title: Executive Summary
text:
11. Claim Severity

Key insight:

Claim severity is strongly right-skewed
Median severity is around 498
Mean severity is higher at around 849
Standard deviation is around 2,936


Claim severity is the main volatility concern. The distribution is strongly right-skewed, meaning most claims are relatively small, but a small number of expensive claims pull the mean above the median. The high standard deviation also shows that claim costs vary widely. This matters because even if most policies have no claims, a few severe claims can still affect profitability. Therefore, the insurer should investigate high-severity claims in more detail using claim-level data.

title: Executive Summary
text:
12. Recommendations and Conclusion
Recommendations:

Review comprehensive without excess (COMP_N) policies due to higher loss-making share
Investigate why loss ratio increased from 2022 to 2024
Monitor New Business profitability against Portfolio policies
Investigate the Bad bonus score anomaly
Analyse high-severity claims using more granular claim-level data

Conclusion:
The portfolio remains profitable, but rising loss ratio suggests emerging profitability pressure.

Overall, the portfolio is still profitable, but the rising loss ratio suggests that profitability pressure is emerging. Policy type, business type, bonus score and year show meaningful relationships with profitability. Claim severity appears to be the main source of volatility because a small number of expensive claims can pull average claim cost upward. The insurer should prioritise reviewing COMP_N policies, understanding the worsening loss ratio trend and studying high-severity claims in more detail.
